title: A Very Strong El Niño Could Shake Up Weather Around the World
summary:
Federal forecasters say Earth could be seeing the strongest El Niño on record this year. Some people have nicknamed it "Super El Niño" or even "Godzilla El Niño," NPR reports.

El Niño is a natural climate pattern that happens every two to seven years. It begins when a huge area of water near the equator in the eastern Pacific Ocean warms up. That warm water releases heat into the air, which shifts weather patterns around the planet. Its opposite, called La Niña, happens when that water is cooler than usual.

Daniel Vimont, a scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, compares El Niño to dropping an enormous rock into a pond. Even places far from where the rock lands still feel the waves.

Forecasters at NOAA, the U.S. government's weather and ocean agency, say this year's event fits the "very strong" category. That means ocean water in a key area off South America is more than 2 degrees Celsius warmer than average. El Niños usually peak in November and December, but this one is already the strongest ever measured for this time of year. Forecasters expect it to last into early 2027.

El Niño years tend to be extra hot worldwide, and experts say temperature records could fall in 2027. Climate change, caused mainly by burning fossil fuels, is also warming the planet.

In the United States, southern states often get heavier rain during El Niño. That can raise flood risks, but it can also help refill water supplies in the dry Southwest. Northern states tend to be warmer and drier. El Niño can also mean fewer hurricanes in the Atlantic Ocean.

Scientists say El Niño "loads the dice" for certain kinds of weather, but it does not guarantee what will happen in every place.
why_it_matters: A record El Niño could affect rain, floods, droughts and temperatures in the U.S. and around the world, so understanding it helps people prepare.
